commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied here tests whether defining the problem, business need, strategic alignment, and accountable owner before selecting an AI tool changes outcomes, and no study documents the hazard of solution-driven adoption. Support for the recommendation rests on endorsements from frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries, which reflect expert agreement rather than measured effect.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The endorsements are mostly commentaries and consensus guidance. One cited CHAI playbook excerpt concerns cybersecurity evaluation rather than problem definition, which suggests the stated count of 14 endorsements may overstate direct support.

The hazard of adopting AI that meets no real need and has no accountable owner is described in endorsements but not measured in any supplied study. Without data, it remains unknown how often unowned or poorly targeted tools lead to patient harm, or whether upfront problem definition intercepts those failures before deployment.

Several commentaries argue that limited resources require choosing use cases carefully, and one describes a single-center selection process. These accounts describe how organizations say they prioritize, but none reports costs, staff time, or whether prioritization reduced abandoned or unused tools. Leaders adopting the practice would be relying on reasoning rather than measured return.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI selection with and without a documented problem statement, business case, and named accountable owner. Useful designs would track tool uptake, abandonment, time to value, safety events, and cost across health systems that do and do not apply structured intake and prioritization before procurement.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether problem-prioritization processes surface the needs of these patients or whether organizations rank their problems lower, which would require deliberate inclusion of these groups in the primary research that the CHAI guide describes.
